Sparsity priors

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-sparsity-priors.Rmd
methods-sparsity-priors.Rmd

em() integrates random effects whose deviations are exactly zero unless the data need them. gr(group, dist = ) in an effect formula sets the distribution:

distribution deviation \(\eta\) of a group hyperparameters
spikeSlab() \(0\) with probability \(1 - \rho\), else \(\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\) prob_<grouping>, tau_<grouping>
dirichletProcess() value of the cluster of the group: \(0\) for the population cluster, else one \(\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\) draw per cluster concentration_<grouping>, tau_<grouping>

The spike and slab decides for every group alone whether it deviates. The Dirichlet process also groups the groups: the groups of one cluster share one deviation, so a fit tells which groups behave alike, not only which differ from the population value.

Guide: Sparse deviations; normal random effects: Marginal likelihood of mixed-effects models.

Approximate marginal

\(D_i(\eta_i)\) is the data \(-2 \log L\) of group \(i\), summed over the conditions of the group. The random effects of a group split into normal coordinates \(N\) and sparse ones \(S\).

Joint mode

em() first finds the joint mode \(\hat\eta\), minimizing

\[\begin{aligned} \Phi(\eta) = {} & \sum_i \Bigl[ D_i(\eta_i) + \eta_{iN}^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_{iN} \Bigr] + \sum_{\text{spike and slab, Dirichlet}} \frac{\eta^2}{\tau^2} : \end{aligned} \tag{1}\]

data, normal prior, and the slab alone for spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process coordinates. Each group is minimized separately by trust(), on Gauss-Newton plus a BFGS correction from the points that lowered \(\Phi\) (Gauss-Newton alone overestimates the curvature at large residuals). The mode is smooth in the parameters, so the marginal does not jump where the most probable structure changes. Random effects that reach no data rest at 0 (Reported structure).

inner search rule
start modes of the last accepted point, moved to first order along the step (Exact gradient)
tolerance ftol and mtol of the tolControl of the outer trust region where given, else \(10^{-10}\); gtol where given, else that of trust()
local minima start from the lowest of the current mode and the minima at the last four distinct accepted points, since the lowest outweighs a higher one by \(e^{\Delta\Phi / 2}\)
restarts at the start and every 25 accepted steps also from 0 and from two fixed moves by the slab standard deviation; em() draws no random numbers

Normal coordinates

The data term is expanded to second order at the mode, with gradient \(\nabla D_i\) and Gauss-Newton curvature \(H_i\). \(H_{NN}\) is the normal block plus \(2 \Omega^{-1}\), the curvature of the Laplace approximation. The normal coordinates integrate out exactly on the quadratic model, leaving the volume \(\log \lvert H_{NN}/2 \rvert\) and for the sparse coordinates the Schur complement

\[\tilde H_i = H_{SS} - H_{SN} H_{NN}^{-1} H_{NS}, \tag{2}\]

so the data term on the sparse coordinates is, up to a constant, \(\exp(-\tfrac12 \eta_{iS}^\top P_i\, \eta_{iS} + b_i^\top \eta_{iS})\) with

\[P_i = \tilde H_i / 2, \qquad b_i = \tfrac12 \bigl( \tilde H_i\, \hat\eta_{iS} - \nabla_S D_i \bigr) \tag{3}\]

Unlike in FOCEI, \(P_i\) holds no prior; the sparse prior enters the integral \(I\) exactly. \(P_i\) may be singular where the data do not see a coordinate; the integral needs no inverse.

Value of the marginal

\[\begin{aligned} -2 \log L \approx {} & \sum_i \Bigl[ D_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log \lvert H_{NN}/2 \rvert + \tfrac12 \hat\eta_{iS}^\top \tilde H_i\, \hat\eta_{iS} - \nabla_S D_i^\top \hat\eta_{iS} \\ & \qquad + \hat\eta_{iN}^\top \Omega^{-1} \hat\eta_{iN} \Bigr] + G \log \lvert \Omega \rvert - 2 \log I + D_0 , \end{aligned} \tag{4}\]

\(D_0\) the \(-2 \log L\) of conditions without random effects and of other terms such as priors, and

\[I = \int \prod_i \exp\Bigl( -\tfrac12\, \eta_{iS}^\top P_i\, \eta_{iS} + b_i^\top \eta_{iS} \Bigr)\, p(\eta_S)\, d\eta_S \tag{5}\]

\(p\) the sparse prior. Without sparse coordinates (4) is the FOCEI value. Every structure, a subset of spike coordinates or a partition into clusters, is a Gaussian integral. Spike-and-slab priors factor over groups, the Dirichlet process couples the groups of a symbol, and off-diagonal entries of \(P_i\) couple the coordinates of a group.

Factor integrals

\(I\) is evaluated in exactly integrated factors:

  • every Dirichlet-process symbol, all groups jointly;
  • the spike-and-slab symbols of a group jointly, within a budget of terms, beyond it each alone.

A factor is integrated against a tilt \(\exp(h^\top \eta - \tfrac12 \eta^\top T \eta)\), \(T = P_{ff}\) uncoupled, diagonal under the expectation consistent (EC) approximation; \(T = 0\) needs no special case. By Fisher’s identity,

\[\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial h} = \mathbb{E}\, \eta, \qquad \frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial T} = -\tfrac12\, \mathbb{E}\, \eta \eta^\top, \tag{6}\]

and a hyperparameter derivative is the posterior expectation of the derivative of the log prior.

Spike and slab

The prior [1], [2] is a point mass at 0 of weight \(1 - \rho\) and a normal slab of weight \(\rho\). With \(V_F = (T_{FF} + \tau^{-2} \mathbb{1})^{-1}\) for the subset \(F\) of slab coordinates,

\[Z = \sum_F \rho^{|F|} (1 - \rho)^{K - |F|}\, \frac{\lvert V_F \rvert^{1/2}}{\tau^{|F|}}\, \exp\bigl( \tfrac12 h_F^\top V_F\, h_F \bigr) , \tag{7}\]

\(2^K\) Gaussian integrals, the factors \(2\pi\) canceling. \(\Pr(F \mid y)\) is the term of \(F\) over \(Z\); given \(F\), \(\eta_F \sim \mathcal{N}(V_F h_F, V_F)\) and the rest is 0. The mixture has

\[\begin{aligned} 1 - p_{0k} &= \sum_{F \ni k} \Pr(F \mid y), \\ \mathbb{E}\, \eta &= \sum_F \Pr(F \mid y)\, \mu_F, \\ \mathbb{E}\, \eta \eta^\top &= \sum_F \Pr(F \mid y) \bigl( V_F + \mu_F \mu_F^\top \bigr), \end{aligned} \tag{8}\]

\(\mu_F\), \(V_F\) zero-filled outside \(F\); the second moment is full within the factor. Summed over coordinates sharing them,

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial \rho} &= \sum_k \Bigl( \frac{1 - p_{0k}}{\rho} - \frac{p_{0k}}{1 - \rho} \Bigr), \\ \frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial \tau} &= \sum_k \Bigl( -\frac{1 - p_{0k}}{\tau} + \frac{\mathbb{E}\, \eta_k^2}{\tau^3} \Bigr) . \end{aligned} \tag{9}\]

The sum is a depth-first search, each coordinate in or out:

element rule
cost per term \(O(K^2)\): including a coordinate adds one row to \(W = L^{-1}\), \(L\) the Cholesky factor of \(V_F^{-1}\)
second moment \(V_F = W^\top W\); each included coordinate adds the outer product of the new row times the weight of all terms below; means and rows enter by a symmetric rank-\(k\) update
pruning subtree skipped where a bound falls below \(e^{-40}\) of the largest term, at most \(2^K e^{-40}\) of \(Z\); the bound uses the subset of slab and open coordinates and the conditional precisions as lower bounds on later diagonal entries of \(L\)
order branch with the larger bound first
single coordinate needs only \(t > -\tau^{-2}\)
limit \(2^{24}\) nodes, beyond which the group goes to EC with one factor per coordinate

Clusters

A Dirichlet-process symbol integrates by a recursion over subsets of the groups (Partition sum).

Expectation consistent approximation

Where no Dirichlet-process symbol joins two groups, the groups are integrated one by one, a group exactly where the data do not couple the factors of the group and the joint spike-and-slab sum stays within the budget. Where a Dirichlet-process symbol joins two groups, all groups are integrated together, exactly where this holds for every group. Otherwise \(I\) is the EC approximation [3], of the group, or of all groups where they are integrated together. With the coupling \(\mathcal{G}(\eta) = \prod_i \exp(-\tfrac12 \eta_i^\top P_i \eta_i + b_i^\top \eta_i)\) and the statistics \(\phi(\eta) = (\eta_k, -\eta_k^2/2)_k\):

  • \(q \propto p\, e^{\lambda^\top \phi}\), every factor exact against a diagonal cavity \(\lambda\);
  • \(r \propto \mathcal{G}\, e^{\gamma^\top \phi}\), the coupling exact under diagonal sites \(\gamma\), a Gaussian of precision \(P_i + \operatorname{diag}(\gamma_t)\) per group.

With \(A_q(\lambda) = \log \int p\, e^{\lambda^\top \phi}\), \(A_r(\gamma) = \log \int \mathcal{G}\, e^{\gamma^\top \phi}\) and the product of one-dimensional Gaussians \(A_s(\nu) = \log \int e^{\nu^\top \phi}\),

\[\log I \;\approx\; A_q(\lambda) + A_r(\gamma) - A_s(\nu), \qquad \nu = \lambda + \gamma, \tag{10}\]

where \(q\), \(r\) and \(e^{\nu^\top \phi}\) agree in mean and variance of every coordinate. The cavity is the self-consistent field of the other factors. The result is exact without coupling and for Gaussian factors, and no bound.

A double loop converges for any coupling [4]. The outer step sets \(\nu_t = 1 / \operatorname{Var}\, \eta_k\), \(\nu_h = \mathbb{E}\, \eta_k / \operatorname{Var}\, \eta_k\). The inner loop minimizes the convex

\[\Psi_\nu(\lambda) = A_q(\lambda) + A_r(\nu - \lambda), \tag{11}\]

by Newton steps on \(\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi + \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi\) with backtracking, quadratically convergent. \(\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi\) includes third and fourth factor moments, and for a Dirichlet-process symbol of up to ten groups the moments between groups, so a step solves all coordinates jointly. The cavity is the variable, so no cavity precision is a difference \(1 / \operatorname{Var}_r \eta_k - \gamma_{t,k}\), and site precisions may be negative. Steps stay in the domains: Gaussian part positive definite (Cholesky of the Jacobi-scaled precision), \(\lambda_t > -\tau^{-2}\) for slab coordinates, \(\tau^{-2} + \sum_g \min(\lambda_{t,g}, 0) > 0\) for a Dirichlet-process symbol. Evaluations start from the last accepted sites.

The outer fixed-point step converges linearly, slowly for tight coupling, so the outer loop takes Newton steps on \(\mathbb{E}_q \phi(\lambda^*(\nu)) = \mathbb{E}_s \phi(\nu)\), \(s \propto e^{\nu^\top \phi}\). With \(\mathrm{d}\lambda^* = (\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi + \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi)^{-1} \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi\; \mathrm{d}\nu\) from the inner stationarity, the Jacobian is

\[\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi\, (\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi + \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi)^{-1} \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi - \operatorname{Cov}_s \phi , \tag{12}\]

solved with row and column scaling, since pinned coordinates have tiny second moments. The cavities move with \(\mathrm{d}\lambda^*\), starting the next inner loop near the solution.

loop ends
inner means within \(10^{-10}\) standard deviations and variances within \(10^{-10}\) relative; or within \(10^{-4}\) when Newton no longer lowers \(\Psi\)
outer marginals of \(r\) match the Gaussians of \(\nu\) to \(10^{-10}\); or within \(10^{-4}\) when a fixed-point step no longer raises the free energy \(F = A_q + A_r - A_s\) (rounding of an ill-conditioned Gaussian part)
outer Newton step accepted where it raises \(F\) by the Armijo condition, the step halved down to a sixteenth; else the fixed-point step, which always raises \(F\)
failure a failed evaluation; the trust region shortens the step

fit$coupling is "expectationConsistent" where a group needed it, NULL otherwise.

Exact gradient

At the fixed point the value is stationary in sites and cavities, so derivatives hold them fixed. For exact factors, Fisher’s identity gives

\[\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial b_i} = \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS}, \qquad \frac{\partial \log I}{\partial P_i} = -\tfrac12 \bigl( \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS}\, \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS}^\top + \Sigma_i \bigr), \tag{13}\]

\(\Sigma_i\) the posterior covariance, block diagonal over factors. Under EC, \(\mathbb{E}\) is \(\mathbb{E}_r\), \(\Sigma_i\) the covariance of \(r\), full within the group, and hyperparameter derivatives are taken per factor at the cavity.

Through (3), with \(\delta_i = \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS} - \hat\eta_{iS}\), the derivatives of \(-2 \log L\) in \(\nabla_S D_i\), \(\tilde H_i\) and the mode are

\[\delta_i, \qquad \tfrac12 \bigl( \delta_i \delta_i^\top + \Sigma_i \bigr), \qquad -\tilde H_i\, \delta_i - \nabla_S D_i , \tag{14}\]

and through (2) those in \(H_i\) and \(\Omega\). The chain then needs \(\partial \nabla D_i / \partial \psi\) from the exact data Hessian, \(\partial H_i / \partial \psi\) and \(\partial H_i / \partial \eta\) from second derivatives as for the FOCEI volume term, and the mode shift.

The mode moves in all coordinates, normal, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process. The inner stationarity \(\nabla_\eta \Phi = 0\) gives

\[\frac{d \hat\eta}{d \psi} = -\bigl( \nabla^2_\eta \Phi \bigr)^{-1} \nabla^2_{\eta \psi} \Phi , \tag{15}\]

group by group. The derivative of the slab gradient in \(\tau\), \(-4 \eta / \tau^3\), gives the mode shift in \(\tau\); \(\rho\) and \(\alpha\) do not move the mode. The shift also starts the inner search at the next trial point. The gradient is exact for the approximate marginal.

Hyperparameters

E-step

Every evaluation of the marginal is an E-step; the M-steps set the hyperparameter curvature of the joint trust region. EM in general: EM algorithm. The objective is \(-2Q\), \(Q\) the expected complete-data log-density.

With the indicator \(z_{ik}\) (1 slab, 0 spike), the complete-data \(-2 \log\) prior over groups \(i\) and symbols \(k\) is, up to terms free of \(\rho\) and \(\tau\),

\[\begin{aligned} -2 \log p(\eta, z \mid \rho, \tau) = \sum_{i,k} \Bigl[ & -2 z_{ik} \log \rho - 2 (1 - z_{ik}) \log (1 - \rho) \\ & + z_{ik} \Bigl( 2 \log \tau + \frac{\eta_{ik}^2}{\tau^2} \Bigr) \Bigr] . \end{aligned} \tag{16}\]

The posterior expectation is

\[\begin{aligned} -2Q(\rho, \tau) = {} & -2 \bar n \log \rho - 2 (n - \bar n) \log (1 - \rho) \\ & + 2 \bar n \log \tau + \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\tau^2} , \end{aligned} \tag{17}\]

\(n\) the number of deviations of the term, and the statistics

\[\begin{aligned} \bar n &= \sum_{i,k} \mathbb{E}\, z_{ik} = \sum_{i,k} (1 - p_{0,ik}), \\ \mathbb{E} \sum v^2 &= \sum_{i,k} \mathbb{E}\, z_{ik} \eta_{ik}^2 = \sum_{i,k} \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{ik}^2 , \end{aligned} \tag{18}\]

since \(\eta_{ik} = 0\) wherever \(z_{ik} = 0\). The expectations are under the posterior of the approximate marginal, the quadratic model at the joint mode (Normal coordinates) times the exact prior, independent over groups:

\[p(\eta_{iS} \mid y_i) \propto \exp\Bigl( -\tfrac12\, \eta_{iS}^\top P_i\, \eta_{iS} + b_i^\top \eta_{iS} \Bigr) \prod_k p(\eta_{ik}) , \tag{19}\]

The spike-and-slab symbols of a group form one factor (Spike and slab), exact on \((P_i, b_i)\) without coupled sparse coordinates. Under EC each coordinate is a factor on a one-dimensional Gaussian of precision \(a\) and center \(m\), a sum of two terms, with slab posterior

\[V = \frac{1}{a + \tau^{-2}}, \qquad \mu = V a\, m . \tag{20}\]

deviation probability

\[1 - p_0 = \operatorname{logit}^{-1} \Bigl( \operatorname{logit} \rho + \frac{\mu^2}{2 V} + \tfrac12 \log \frac{V}{\tau^2} \Bigr) : \tag{21}\]

prior log odds, exponent gain at the slab mean, and log width ratio. The moments are

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\, \eta &= (1 - p_0)\, \mu, \\ \mathbb{E}\, \eta^2 &= (1 - p_0)\, (\mu^2 + V), \\ \operatorname{Var} \eta &= \mathbb{E}\, \eta^2 - (\mathbb{E}\, \eta)^2 . \end{aligned} \tag{22}\]

Here \(a = a^c_{ik}\), \(m = m^c_{ik}\) is the cavity (EC); the moments are those of \(q\), equal to those of \(r\) at the fixed point, and \(\Sigma_i = (P_i + \operatorname{diag} \gamma_{t,i})^{-1}\) with the site precisions \(\gamma_{t,i}\) of the group.

Given the sparse coordinates, on the expansion

\[\begin{aligned} \eta_{iN} \mid \eta_{iS} &\sim \mathcal{N}\bigl( \hat\eta_{iN} - R_i\, (\eta_{iS} - \hat\eta_{iS}),\; 2 H_{NN}^{-1} \bigr), \\ R_i &= H_{NN}^{-1} H_{NS} , \end{aligned} \tag{23}\]

so fit$etaCov, the posterior covariance of all random effects of the group, has the blocks

\[\Sigma_{NN} = 2 H_{NN}^{-1} + R_i \Sigma_{SS} R_i^\top, \qquad \Sigma_{NS} = -R_i \Sigma_{SS} , \tag{24}\]

and se of fit$random is the square root of the diagonal. \(\Omega\) has no M-step; it moves with the fixed parameters.

By Fisher’s identity the derivative of \(-2 \log I\) at the current point is that of \(-2Q\),

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial (-2Q)}{\partial \rho} &= -2 \Bigl( \frac{\bar n}{\rho} - \frac{n - \bar n}{1 - \rho} \Bigr), \\ \frac{\partial (-2Q)}{\partial \tau} &= 2 \Bigl( \frac{\bar n}{\tau} - \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\tau^3} \Bigr), \end{aligned} \tag{25}\]

the marginal gradient in \(\tau\) adding the mode shift (Exact gradient).

M-steps

The closed-form M-step of a hyperparameter minimizes \(-2Q\) at the current posterior moments; the complete data are \((\eta, z)\) for the spike and slab and partition plus cluster values for the Dirichlet process. With \(n\) the number of deviations of a term (groups times symbols), \(\bar n\) the expected number of slab deviations or of clusters off the population value, and \(\mathbb{E} \sum v^2\) the expected sum of their squares,

\[\tau^2 = \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\bar n}, \qquad \rho = \frac{\bar n}{n}, \qquad \bar n = \sum_k \sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + i} , \tag{26}\]

the last for the concentration, summed over the symbols \(k\) of the term; the sum increases in \(\alpha\), and Newton’s method on \(\log \alpha\) solves it.

Near the optimum an M-step is a gradient step scaled by the complete-data information \(\mathcal{I}_c\), while the data hold \(\mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} = \mathcal{I}_c - \mathcal{I}_{\text{mis}}\). The error shrinks per iteration by the fraction of missing information [5],

\[\mathcal{I}_c^{-1} \mathcal{I}_{\text{mis}} , \tag{27}\]

close to one for a hyperparameter from a few groups. Newton on the curvature of \(-2Q\) is worse far from the optimum: on \(u = \log \tau\) with M-step \(u^* = \tfrac12 \log(\mathbb{E} \sum v^2 / \bar n)\) it steps \(\bigl(1 - e^{-2(u^* - u)}\bigr) / 2\), which is \(0.5\) for \(u^*\) five above and \(-11013\) for five below.

Joint trust region

em() moves fixed parameters and hyperparameters, on \(\log \tau\), \(\log \alpha\), \(\operatorname{logit} \rho\), in one trust region with the exact marginal gradient.

For the fixed parameters the model Hessian is the Schur complement over all random effects, the sparse ones at the curvature of their posterior: a factor with posterior covariance \(\Sigma\) and data curvature \(\tilde H_{ff}\) gets the prior curvature \(2 \Sigma^{-1} - \tilde H_{ff}\), so the block of the factor after eliminating the normal coordinates is \(2 \Sigma^{-1}\); under EC the prior curvature is \(2 \operatorname{diag}(\gamma_t)\), negative site precisions set to 0. The data Hessian blocks are all Gauss-Newton (forward over reverse), making the Schur complement positive semidefinite, or all exact (second-order sensitivities); mixed blocks can be far from definite. Exact rows enter gradient and mode shift. With normal random effects alone this is the FOCEI Schur complement.

For every hyperparameter the model Hessian is the secant to the M-step,

\[\kappa_h = \frac{\partial_u (-2Q)}{u - u^*}, \tag{28}\]

with

\[\partial_u (-2Q) = \begin{cases} 2 \bigl( \bar n - \mathbb{E} \sum v^2 / \tau^2 \bigr) & \text{for } \tau, \\ -2 \, (\bar n - n \rho) & \text{for } \rho, \\ -2 \bigl( \bar n - \sum_k \sum_{i=1}^{G} \alpha / (\alpha + i) \bigr) & \text{for } \alpha . \end{cases} \tag{29}\]

\(-2Q\) is convex in \(u\), so \(\kappa_h > 0\); at \(u = u^*\), \(\kappa_h\) is the complete-data information

\[\partial_u^2 (-2Q) = \begin{cases} 4\, \mathbb{E} \sum v^2 / \tau^2 & \text{for } \tau, \\ 2 n \rho (1 - \rho) & \text{for } \rho, \\ 2 \sum_k \sum_{i=1}^{G} \alpha\, i / (\alpha + i)^2 & \text{for } \alpha , \end{cases} \tag{30}\]

and \(\kappa_h \ge 10^{-8}\). A Newton step on \(\kappa_h\) alone moves \(u\) by

\[\Delta u = -\frac{1}{\kappa_h} \frac{\partial (-2 \log L)}{\partial u} = u^* - u - \frac{1}{\kappa_h}\, \nabla_{\hat\eta} (-2 \log L)^\top \frac{d \hat\eta}{d u} , \tag{31}\]

with the mode shift \(d \hat\eta / d u\) of Exact gradient: the exact M-step for \(\rho\) and \(\alpha\), plus a term for \(\tau\) that vanishes where the data term is quadratic in the random effects.

A BFGS correction learns the missing information and the cross curvature [6], [7] from every step between two points that lowered \(-2 \log L\). Pairs with \(0 < s^\top y \le 10^{-8} \lVert s \rVert \lVert y \rVert\) are skipped; a pair with \(s^\top y \le 0\), or an update that would make the model indefinite, drops the correction. Far from the optimum a step is an EM step in the hyperparameters and a Gauss-Newton step in the fixed parameters, at one marginal evaluation; near it the model approaches the marginal Hessian and convergence is superlinear. Gradient and bounded Hessian suffice for convergence [8], and no number of EM iterations is chosen.

The trust region stops at a predicted reduction below mtol; a run ending short of it restarts with a fresh correction while runs lower \(-2 \log L\) by more than mtol. msem() multistarts with concentrations and slab standard deviations perturbed on the log scale, slab probabilities on the logit scale. No model Hessian is the marginal Hessian, so fit$hessian is NULL and standard errors come from the group scores (Standard errors).

Reported structure

The fit reports the most probable structure: the most probable subset per spike-and-slab factor, the most probable partition per Dirichlet-process symbol (the partition recursion with maximum for sum). Spike deviations are exactly zero. A slab deviation is the slab mean given that structure: in a joint factor \(\mu_{F^*} = V_{F^*} b_{F^*}\); for a coordinate alone or under EC, \(\mu = V a\, m\) (E-step) where \(1 - p_0 > \tfrac12\), at the cavity under EC. Free clusters take the posterior mean given the partition.

column of fit$random content
mode this value
se posterior standard deviation over spike and slab
cluster 0 for the population value, 1, 2, … for deviating groups or clusters in group order (spike and slab, Dirichlet process)
p0 posterior probability of a zero deviation (spike and slab, Dirichlet process)
data whether the random effect reaches data of the group, where some do not

Before the fit, em() traces every sparse random effect through parameter transformations, steady states, right-hand sides, events, observables and error model to the measured names of the group, a search in the symbol graph with the names that are 0 in the condition set to 0. A product with a zero factor vanishes; a state that starts at 0, whose right-hand side vanishes with the other zeros and that no event moves, stays 0 by uniqueness of the solution. A steady-state root depends on an input only through the states whose equations or conservation rows the input reaches, directly or through moved states, where the remaining subsystem has full structural rank, and through every root otherwise. No path means a sensitivity of 0 for all parameter values.

A random effect without data rests at 0: no mode search, integral factor 1, no part in the hyperparameter updates, reported with the prior standard deviation, for a Dirichlet-process one with the slab standard deviation \(\tau\), and, for the spike and slab, \(p_0 = 1 - \rho\). A Dirichlet-process group without data leaves the partition without changing the others, since the Ewens prior of a subset is that of the subset. This removes flat directions of mode and integral.

fit$slab lists the probabilities, concentrations and slab standard deviations, each with the symbols, the estimate and whether it was fixed.

Selection of deviations

Choosing deviations is a choice among \(2^K\) structures per group. A likelihood-ratio test per coordinate depends on which others are free and, for coupled coordinates, on the test order.

An L1 penalty \(\lambda \sum \lvert \eta \rvert\) [9], as in trustL1(), sets small deviations to 0, shrinks every selected one by the same amount, and compensates by selecting more small ones. Of coordinates the data tie together it keeps one, unstably, since the lasso condition for the right set fails for such correlations. It gives no probability of a deviation.

The spike and slab separates decision and size: a deviation is 0 or from the slab, which shrinks little, and (7) weighs every structure by the marginal likelihood, with \(\rho\) and \(\tau\) estimated instead of scanned. Coupled coordinates the data cannot separate share the posterior, with intermediate \(p_0\). Both statements hold within the Laplace approximation of the data term.

Groups that deviate alike are a second structure. The Dirichlet process (Dirichlet-process random effects) weighs every partition of the groups into clusters with one common deviation by the marginal likelihood, the population value one of the clusters. The penalized counterpart is the clustered lasso [10], a penalty on the pairwise differences of the group parameters, for which Hauber et al. favor the exponent 0.8 over the L1 norm; fuse of trustL1() is the L1 form: groups with equal values move as one, and without an anchor no group is the reference. Like the L1 penalty it is scanned over the penalty strength and gives no probability of a cluster.

Where the data leave fixed-effect directions flat, the fixed-effect prior decides between equally good structures, and the selection moves with the width of that prior. Only a model reduced to what the data determine resolves this.

Standard errors

With spike-and-slab random effects, \(-2 \log L = -2 \sum_i \log L_i + D_0\). Mode, curvature and integral of a group depend on the data of that group alone, and the mode shift is block diagonal, so the exact gradient splits into the group gradients. With the scores \(s_i = \nabla \log L_i\) and their mean \(\bar s\), the empirical information is

\[\mathcal{I} = \frac{G}{G - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{G} (s_i - \bar s)(s_i - \bar s)^\top + \tfrac12 H_0 , \tag{32}\]

\(H_0\) the Hessian of \(D_0\), priors included; fit$information holds it, vcov() inverts it. At the optimum the scores sum to \(\tfrac12 \nabla D_0\), which the centering removes: the first term has rank at most \(G - 1\), and \(H_0\) must cover the remaining directions. Otherwise vcov() is an error and standard errors are NA. In the guide fit, five compounds give rank at most four, and the conditions without a compound and the prior give the rest. Under dirichletProcess() the marginal is no sum over groups, so there is neither Hessian nor empirical information; confint(method = "profile") gives intervals.

Dirichlet-process random effects

gr(group, dist = dirichletProcess()) lets groups share deviations: groups and the population value, the anchor, form clusters; the anchor cluster has deviation zero, every other one a common slab deviation \(\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\). The reported partition is a grouping of the groups by their behavior, found by the fit rather than given. \(\alpha\) and \(\tau\) are estimated by marginal maximum likelihood, without a penalty scan. The reported structure is that of the spike and slab with clusters for deviations. The guide compounds are fitted without it.

Ewens prior

The partitions \(\mathcal{C}\) of the \(G\) groups and the anchor follow the Ewens distribution [11] of the Chinese restaurant process, anchor seated first: a group joins a cluster with probability proportional to the size, anchor counted, or opens one with probability proportional to \(\alpha\),

\[\Pr(\mathcal{C}) = \frac{\alpha^{\lvert \mathcal{C} \rvert - 1} \prod_{T \in \mathcal{C}} (\lvert T \rvert - 1)!} {\prod_{i=1}^{G} (\alpha + i)} , \tag{33}\]

\(\lvert \mathcal{C} \rvert\) the number of clusters, \(\lvert T \rvert\) their sizes. The prior depends on the sizes only: it is exchangeable, independent of the data, and consistent in \(G\). \(\alpha \to 0\) puts every group at the population value, \(\alpha \to \infty\) in separate clusters; the expected number of free clusters is \(\sum_{i=1}^{G} \alpha / (\alpha + i)\).

Partition sum

The data term is expanded at the mode under the slab alone. Per symbol, on the group factors \(\exp(-\tfrac12 a_i \eta^2 + b_i \eta)\) of the natural form (5), a cluster \(T\) with

\[A_T = \sum_{i \in T} a_i, \qquad B_T = \sum_{i \in T} b_i \tag{34}\]

has the weight

\[w(T) = (\lvert T \rvert - 1)! \tag{35}\]

with the anchor, at deviation 0, and without it, the cluster value integrated over the slab,

\[w(T) = \alpha\, (\lvert T \rvert - 1)!\; \bigl(1 + \tau^2 A_T\bigr)^{-1/2} \exp\Bigl( \frac{B_T^2}{2 (A_T + \tau^{-2})} \Bigr) . \tag{36}\]

With \(\mathcal{Z}(X)\) the sum over the partitions of \(X\) of the products of cluster weights,

\[\mathcal{Z}(X) = \sum_{T \subseteq X,\ \min X \in T} w(T)\, \mathcal{Z}(X \setminus T), \qquad I = \frac{\mathcal{Z}(U)}{\prod_{i=1}^{G} (\alpha + i)} , \tag{37}\]

\(3^{G+1}\) terms, exact for up to 14 groups. \(T\) is a cluster with probability \(w(T)\, \mathcal{Z}(U \setminus T) / \mathcal{Z}(U)\), a free cluster value then normal with mean \(B_T / (A_T + \tau^{-2})\) and variance \(1 / (A_T + \tau^{-2})\); moments, \(p_0\), M-step statistics and derivatives follow. The most probable partition uses maximum for sum.

Gradient and M-steps

From the posterior moments,

\[\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial \alpha} = \frac{\bar n}{\alpha} - \sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{1}{\alpha + i}, \qquad \frac{\partial \log I}{\partial \tau} = -\frac{\bar n}{\tau} + \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\tau^3} , \tag{38}\]

\(\bar n\) the expected number of free clusters, \(\mathbb{E} \sum v^2\) the expected sum of their squares; the chain through \(\nabla D_i\), \(H_i\) and the mode is as above. The mode shifts with \(\tau\), not \(\alpha\). The M-steps are those of M-steps, summed over symbols.

SAEM

The exact partition sum is limited to 14 groups; method = "saem" draws the partition instead, with normal random effects beside the Dirichlet-process ones and no other sparse ones. Groups start in separate clusters at the slab-only mode, so the sampler merges clusters. Per iteration:

  • Normal random effects. nMcmc random-walk Metropolis steps, step size adapted in burn-in toward acceptance 0.4.
  • Clusters. One Gibbs sweep per symbol, Neal’s algorithm 8 with two auxiliary clusters [12]: each group, in random order, joins an existing cluster with probability proportional to size (anchor counted) times likelihood at the cluster value, or an auxiliary one with a slab draw with probability proportional to \(\alpha / 2\) times likelihood. A group alone offers the current cluster value as one auxiliary. One prediction gives the likelihoods of all groups at one value.
  • Cluster values. Three joint random-walk Metropolis steps, accepted per cluster on the data of the groups in the cluster and the slab.
  • A-step and M-steps. Robbins-Monro averages of the free-cluster count and squared values give \(\tau\) and \(\alpha\); in burn-in they change by a factor in \([0.95, 1.25]\) per iteration and the variances of \(\Omega\) shrink at most 5 %. The rest moves as in SAEM.
phase rule
burn-in ends when no parameter drifts over window iterations, or after nBurnin; converged reports which
averaging nEM iterations, step sizes \(k^{-0.7}\); estimate the mean after the first window
structure most frequent partition after that window, cluster values averaged over the draws with that partition, \(p_0\) the share of draws at the population value

Importance sampling

The \(-2 \log L\) of an SAEM fit comes from sequential importance sampling under the expansion [13]. A particle seats the groups in turn; group \(i\) joins a cluster of every symbol, existing or new, with probability proportional to the Ewens prior times the predictive density given the seated groups, the cluster values having a joint normal posterior. With \(\mathcal{C}_{i-1}\) the partition after \(i - 1\) groups and \(Z(\mathcal{C})\) the integral of the seated factors, the weight is

\[\zeta = \prod_{i=1}^{G} \sum_{T} \Pr(T \mid \mathcal{C}_{i-1})\, \frac{Z(\mathcal{C}_{i-1} + T)}{Z(\mathcal{C}_{i-1})} , \tag{39}\]

summed over the seats \(T\) of group \(i\). The mean \(\bar\zeta\) over \(M\) particles is unbiased for \(I\); by the delta method on \(\log \bar\zeta\),

\[\texttt{valueSE} = \frac{2\, \operatorname{sd}(\zeta)}{\sqrt{M}\, \bar\zeta} . \tag{40}\]

The symbols of a group are seated together on the full \(P_i\). control$saem$particles sets \(M\) (500). An SAEM fit has no gradient, Hessian or empirical information.
